summary: We are testing whether a metric closure MST approach (precomputing best direct-or-relay cost for each robot pair, then building MST on robots only) outperforms a simpler full MST + prune heuristic for the Steiner tree relay optimization problem #211. The metric closure exploits the constraint that relay stations cannot connect to each other, making single-relay mediation the only option and the closure exact.
key_points: Arm h-main (metric closure MST): For each robot pair, precompute the cheapest connection — either direct (with S-discount) or via the single best relay station. Build MST on this N×N metric closure, reconstruct actual edges (inserting relays), then run subgraph MST to handle shared relays, prune unnecessary relay leaves, and greedy-insert remaining relays into robot-robot edges. Predicted score: >80.

Arm h-ablation (full MST + prune): Build all valid edges (excluding C-C), run Kruskal's MST over all N+K nodes, iteratively prune relay leaves that don't help connectivity, remove unprofitable degree-2 relays, and greedy-insert unused relays. This isolates whether the metric closure step is the key mechanism. Predicted score: lower than h-main.

Confirmation criteria: h-main scoring significantly higher than h-ablation confirms that the metric closure precomputation is the essential mechanism. If h-ablation matches or beats h-main, the reconstruction/subgraph-MST step in h-main may be introducing errors (e.g., C-C edges, incorrect relay sharing) and needs debugging.

Risk factors to monitor: (1) O(N²·K) metric closure computation may TLE for N=K=1500 (~3.4B ops) — need to verify timing; (2) subgraph MST reconstruction must avoid creating forbidden C-C edges; (3) the greedy relay insertion post-processing should be checked for correctness on edge cases.

Scoring model: The judge computes min(1.0, base_MST_cost / your_cost), so any network cheaper than the robot-only MST baseline gets full marks. Both arms aim to beat the baseline by leveraging relays and S-node discounts.
